## Proposition 6.20
**Statement:** Similar polygons are divided into similar triangles, and into triangles equal in multitude and in the same ratio as the wholes, and the polygon has to the polygon a ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side has to the corresponding  side.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE and FGHKL be similar polygons, and let AB correspond to FG. We must show that they are divided into similar triangles equal in multitude and in the same ratio as the wholes, and that polygon ABCDE has to polygon FGHKL a ratio duplicate of that which AB has to FG.

**Step 2.** Join BE, BD from vertex B in polygon ABCDE, and join GK, GL from vertex G in polygon FGHKL. Since the polygons are similar, by D6.1 their angles are severally equal and the sides about the equal angles are proportional. In particular, angle A equals angle F, and BA:AE = GF:FL.

**Step 3.** Since angle A equals angle F, and the sides about these equal angles are proportional (BA:AE = GF:FL), triangle ABE is equiangular with triangle FGK by 6.6. Hence triangle ABE is similar to triangle FGL by 6.4, and in particular angle ABE equals angle FGL and angle AEB equals angle FLG.

**Step 4.** Since the polygons are similar, angle ABC equals angle FGH (by D6.1). Since angle ABE equals angle FGL (from Step 3), by CN3 the remainder angle EBC equals the remainder angle LGH.

**Step 5.** Since triangles ABE and FGL are similar (Step 3), we have BE:EL = AB:FG (by 6.4, the sides about equal angles are proportional, specifically BE:GL corresponds to AB:FG). Also, since the polygons are similar, AB:FG = BC:GH (by D6.1, the sides about the equal angles are proportional). Therefore BE:GL = BC:GH by 5.11.

**Step 6.** Thus in triangles EBC and LGH, the angle EBC equals angle LGH (Step 4), and the sides about these equal angles are proportional: BE:GL = BC:GH (Step 5). By 6.6, triangle EBC is equiangular with triangle LGH, and hence similar by 6.4. In particular, angle BEC equals angle GLH, and angle BCE equals angle GHL.

**Step 7.** Since the polygons are similar, angle BCD equals angle GHK (by D6.1). Since angle BCE equals angle GHL (Step 6), by CN3 the remainder angle ECD equals the remainder angle LHK.

**Step 8.** From the similarity of triangle EBC and triangle LGH (Step 6), we have BE:GL = EC:LH (by 6.4). From the similarity of the polygons, CD:HK = BC:GH = BE:GL (Step 5 and D6.1). Hence EC:LH = CD:HK by 5.11.

**Step 9.** Thus in triangles ECD and LHK, the angle ECD equals angle LHK (Step 7), and the sides about these equal angles are proportional: EC:LH = CD:HK (Step 8). By 6.6, triangle ECD is equiangular with triangle LHK, and hence similar by 6.4.

**Step 10.** Therefore the similar polygons ABCDE and FGHKL have been divided into similar triangles (ABE similar to FGL, EBC similar to LGH, and ECD similar to LHK), equal in multitude (three each). The same argument extends by induction to polygons of any number of sides: at each stage, the next pair of triangles is shown similar by the same method using 6.6 and CN3.

**Step 11.** We now show the triangles are in the same ratio as the wholes. Since triangle ABE is similar to triangle FGL, triangle ABE has to triangle FGL the duplicate ratio of BE to GL, by 6.19. Since triangle EBC is similar to triangle LGH, triangle EBC has to triangle LGH the duplicate ratio of BE to GL (using 6.19 again, noting BE:GL is the ratio of corresponding sides in these similar triangles as well, since BE corresponds to GL). Therefore triangle ABE : triangle FGL = triangle EBC : triangle LGH, by 5.11.

**Step 12.** Similarly, since triangle EBC is similar to triangle LGH, triangle EBC has to triangle LGH the duplicate ratio of EC to LH, by 6.19. And since triangle ECD is similar to triangle LHK, triangle ECD has to triangle LHK the duplicate ratio of EC to LH, by 6.19. Therefore triangle EBC : triangle LGH = triangle ECD : triangle LHK, by 5.11.

**Step 13.** From Steps 11 and 12, we have triangle ABE : triangle FGL = triangle EBC : triangle LGH = triangle ECD : triangle LHK. Since corresponding components are in the same ratio, by 5.12, the sum of the antecedents is to the sum of the consequents in the same ratio. That is, (triangle ABE + triangle EBC + triangle ECD) : (triangle FGL + triangle LGH + triangle LHK) = triangle ABE : triangle FGL. But the sum of the triangles in each case equals the respective polygon. Therefore polygon ABCDE : polygon FGHKL = triangle ABE : triangle FGL.

**Step 14.** Since triangle ABE is similar to triangle FGL, by 6.19, triangle ABE has to triangle FGL the duplicate ratio of the corresponding side AB to FG. From Step 13, polygon ABCDE has to polygon FGHKL the same ratio as triangle ABE has to triangle FGL. Therefore polygon ABCDE has to polygon FGHKL the duplicate ratio of AB to FG, which is the ratio of corresponding side to corresponding side.

**Step 15.** Therefore similar polygons are divided into similar triangles, equal in multitude and in the same ratio as the wholes, and the polygon has to the polygon a ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side has to the corresponding side. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 5.11, 5.12, 6.19, 6.4, 6.6, CN3, D5.9, D6.1
**Human refs (from References field):** 1.32, 5.12, 5.22, 6.1, 6.19, 6.4, 6.6, D6.1

heath_proof_text: Let ABCDE, FGHKL be similar polygons, and let AB correspond to FG; I say that the polygons ABCDE, FGHKL are divided into similar triangles, and into triangles equal in multitude and inthe same ratio as the wholes, and the polygon ABCDE has to the polygon FGHKL a ratio duplicate of that which AB has to FG. Let BE, EC, GL, LH be joined. Now, since the polygon ABCDE is similar to the polygonFGHKL, the angle BAE is equal to the angle GFL; and, as BA is to AE, so is GF to FL. [VI. Def. 1]  Since then ABE, FGL are two triangles having one angle equal to one angle and the sides about the equal anglesproportional, therefore the triangle ABE is equiangular with the triangle FGL; [VI. 6] so that it is also similar; [VI. 4 and Def. 1]therefore the angle ABE is equal to the angle FGL. But the whole angle ABC is also equal to the whole angle FGH because of the similarity of the polygons; therefore the remaining angle EBC is equal to the angle LGH. And, since, because of the similarity of the triangles ABE,FGL, as EB is to BA, so is LG to GF, and moreover also, because of the similarity of the polygons, as AB is to BC, so is FG to GH, therefore, ex aequali, as EB is to BC, so is LG to GH; [V. 22]that is, the sides about the equal angles EBC, LGH are proportional; therefore the triangle EBC is equiangular with the triangle LGH, [VI. 6] so that the triangle EBC is also similar to the triangle LGH. [VI. 4 and Def. 1]  For the same reason the triangle ECD is also similar to the triangle LHK. Therefore the similar polygons ABCDE, FGHKL have been divided into similar triangles, and into triangles equal inmultitude. I say that they are also in the same ratio as the wholes, that is, in such manner that the triangles are proportional, and ABE, EBC, ECD are antecedents, while FGL, LGH, LHK are their consequents, and that the polygon ABCDE  has to the polygon FGHKL a ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side has to the corresponding side, that is AB to FG. For let AC, FH be joined. Then since, because of the similarity of the polygons,the angle ABC is equal to the angle FGH, and, as AB is to BC, so is FG to GH, the triangle ABC is equiangular with the triangle FGH; [VI. 6]therefore the angle BAC is equal to the angle GFH, and the angle BCA to the angle GHF. And, since the angle BAM is equal to the angle GFN, and the angle ABM is also equal to the angle FGN, therefore the remaining angle AMB is also equal to the remaining angle FNG; [I. 32] therefore the triangle ABM is equiangular with the triangleFGN. Similarly we can prove that the triangle BMC is also equiangular with the triangle GNH. Therefore, proportionally, as AM is to MB, so is FN to NG,and, as BM is to MC, so is GN to NH; so that, in addition, ex aequali, as AM is to MC, so is FN to NH. But, as AM is to MC, so is the triangle ABM to MBC, and AME to EMC; for they are to one another as theirbases. [VI. 1] Therefore also, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents; [V. 12] therefore, as the triangle AMB is to BMC, so is ABE to CBE. But, as AMB is to BMC, so is AM to MC; therefore also, as AM is to MC, so is the triangle ABE to the triangle EBC. For the same reason also, as FN is to NH, so is the triangle FGL to the triangleGLH. And, as AM is to MC, so is FN to NH; therefore also, as the triangle ABE is to the triangle BEC, so is the triangle FGL to the triangle GLH; and, alternately, as the triangle ABE is to the triangle FGL,so is the triangle BEC to the triangle GLH. Similarly we can prove, if BD, GK be joined, that, as the triangle BEC is to the triangle LGH, so also is the triangle ECD to the triangle LHK. And since, as the triangle ABE is to the triangle FGL,so is EBC to LGH, and further ECD to LHK, therefore also, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents so are all the antecedents to all the consequents; [V. 12] therefore, as the triangle ABE is to the triangle FGL, so is the polygon ABCDE to the polygon FGHKL. But the triangle ABE has to the triangle FGL a ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side AB has to the corresponding side FG; for similar triangles are in the duplicate ratio of the corresponding sides. [VI. 19] Therefore the polygon ABCDE also has to the polygonFGHKL a ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side AB has to the corresponding side FG.
